bib.title: AI Engineering, Chapter 1: Introduction to Building AI Applications with Foundation Models

question: Why has AI engineering emerged as a discipline on top of foundation models, what can it be used for, how should one plan an application, and how does the stack differ from ML engineering?
contributions: Traces the path from language models through LLMs and foundation models to AI engineering
Surveys foundation model use cases across consumer and enterprise
Gives planning considerations for AI applications
Describes the three-layer AI engineering stack and contrasts it with ML and full-stack engineering

limits: Overview chapter: the author says it only lightly touches many concepts, deferred to later chapters.
Most numbers are reported from other sources (surveys, press, company reports) and several are uncited or personal communication.
The author's own counts (50 interviews, 205 repos, 920 repos, 20-person survey) are informal and the sample selection is not specified.
Figures such as costs, model sizes (100B is large), and market data are dated to 2023-2024; the author notes large today may be tiny tomorrow.
The claim that ML knowledge is a nice-to-have is flagged by the book as disputed.
practices: Use tokens rather than words or characters as the unit of a language model, because they balance vocabulary size and meaning (Language models, note box).
Frame tasks as completion prompts (translation, spam classification) when using a base language model (Language models).
Pick the adaptation technique by data and effort: prompt engineering needs least data, then finetuning, then training from scratch (Dataset engineering).
Before building, decide why (existential threat, opportunity, hedge) and whether to build or buy (Use Case Evaluation).
Clarify whether AI is critical or complementary, reactive or proactive, dynamic or static, and the role of humans (Planning AI Applications).
Grow automation gradually with Microsoft's Crawl-Walk-Run framework (Planning AI Applications).
Define business metrics and a usefulness threshold across quality, latency (TTFT, TPOT, total), cost and other metrics before shipping (Setting Expectations).
Evaluate existing models first to set milestones, and plan for the last-mile challenge (Milestone Planning).
Keep versioning and evaluation infrastructure so swapping models does not cause headaches (Maintenance).
Compare models under equal prompting conditions, since prompt technique alone changed Gemini Ultra MMLU from 83.7% to 90.04% (Evaluation, Table 1-5).
Build the product first and invest in data and models only once it shows promise (AI Engineering vs Full-Stack Engineering, Fig 1-16).
